topics.title: Nigeria in the 21st Century
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to list key political developments in Nigeria since 2000.
The students should be able to explain major economic changes in 21st century Nigeria.
The students should be able to identify social challenges facing Nigeria in the 21st century.

Introduction:
We have learned about Nigeria's history from pre-colonial times to the end of military rule. Now we will examine how Nigeria has developed in the 21st century, focusing on political, economic, and social aspects.

Content:
The 21st century in Nigeria began with the return to democratic rule in 1999. Politically, Nigeria has experienced several peaceful transitions of power between political parties. In 2007, Umaru Yar'Adua became president after Olusegun Obasanjo, and in 2010, Goodluck Jonathan took over after Yar'Adua's death. In 2015, Muhammadu Buhari became the first opposition candidate to defeat an incumbent president in Nigerian history. In 2023, Bola Ahmed Tinubu was elected as the new president in another peaceful election.

Economically, Nigeria has faced both opportunities and challenges. The country remains Africa's largest economy, heavily dependent on oil revenue which accounts for about 90% of export earnings. However, efforts have been made to diversify the economy through agriculture, technology, and entertainment. The Nollywood film industry has grown significantly, becoming one of the largest film producers in the world. The banking sector has also undergone reforms, leading to stronger financial institutions.

Socially, Nigeria has faced challenges like population growth, which now exceeds 200 million people, making it the most populous country in Africa. The country has also dealt with issues like Boko Haram insurgency in the Northeast, farmer-herder conflicts in the Middle Belt, and occasional ethno-religious tensions. Despite these challenges, Nigeria has made progress in areas like telecommunications, with increased mobile phone usage and internet access transforming how people communicate and do business.

Class activity:
Students will be divided into groups and assigned different decades of the 21st century. Each group will research and present key political, economic, and social developments during their assigned decade.

Evaluation questions:
1. Name three Nigerian presidents who have ruled since 2000.
2. What percentage of Nigeria's export earnings comes from oil?
3. Explain one social challenge facing Nigeria in the 21st century.
4. How has Nigeria's entertainment industry contributed to the country's economy?

Summary:
The 21st century has brought both progress and challenges to Nigeria, with developments in politics, economy, and society shaping the nation's current status as Africa's most populous country and largest economy.

topics.title: Leadership in Contemporary Nigeria
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to list past Nigerian presidents since 1999.
The students should be able to explain the impact of at least two presidents on Nigeria's development.
The students should be able to differentiate between the leadership styles of different Nigerian presidents.

Introduction:
Building on our knowledge of Nigeria's political history, we will now examine the leadership of presidents who have governed Nigeria since the return to democracy in 1999, focusing on their policies and impacts.

Content:
Since 1999, Nigeria has had several presidents who have shaped the country's political and economic landscape. Olusegun Obasanjo served as president from 1999 to 2007, becoming the first civilian president after military rule. His administration focused on debt relief, economic reforms, and the fight against corruption. He initiated the National Economic Empowerment and Development Strategy (NEEDS) to improve the economy and established the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) to combat corruption.

Umaru Yar'Adua served as president from 2007 until his death in 2009. He introduced the Seven-Point Agenda, focusing on power reform, food security, wealth creation, land reform, transportation, education, and security. Yar'Adua also granted amnesty to militants in the Niger Delta, which temporarily reduced oil pipeline vandalism.

Goodluck Jonathan served as president from 2009 to 2015. His administration focused on transforming the agricultural sector through the Agricultural Transformation Agenda and invested in power generation. Jonathan also implemented the Subsidy Reinvestment and Empowerment Program (SURE-P) to utilize funds saved from fuel subsidy removal.

Muhammadu Buhari served as president from 2015 to 2023. His administration focused on anti-corruption efforts, security challenges, and economic diversification. The Buhari government established the Social Investment Programs to support vulnerable Nigerians and made efforts to improve agricultural production through the Anchor Borrowers' Program.

Each president has brought different leadership styles and priorities to governance. Some focused on economic reforms, others on security, and others on anti-corruption measures. The impact of their leadership can be seen in various sectors of Nigerian society, from infrastructure development to changes in the educational system.

Class activity:
Students will create a presentation comparing the leadership styles and key achievements of two different Nigerian presidents since 1999.

Evaluation questions:
1. Name four Nigerian presidents who have ruled since 1999.
2. What was the Seven-Point Agenda introduced by President Yar'Adua?
3. Explain one major anti-corruption measure implemented by President Obasanjo.
4. How did President Jonathan's administration transform the agricultural sector?

Summary:
The leadership of Nigeria's presidents since 1999 has significantly influenced the country's political and economic development, with each leader bringing different priorities and approaches to governance.

topics.title: Federalism in Nigeria
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to define federalism in the Nigerian context.
The students should be able to list at least three challenges of Nigerian federalism.
The students should be able to explain how federalism affects governance in Nigeria.

Introduction:
We have studied Nigeria's political system and leadership. Now we will examine federalism, which is the system of government practiced in Nigeria, and understand its meaning and challenges.

Content:
Federalism is a system of government where power is shared between a central (federal) government and regional (state) governments. In Nigeria, federalism means that both the federal government and the state governments have specific powers and responsibilities defined by the constitution. Nigeria operates a federal system with 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory, Abuja.

The Nigerian federal system has several key features. First, there is a division of powers between the federal, state, and local governments. The federal government handles matters like defense, foreign affairs, currency, and customs. State governments handle matters like education, health, and agriculture. Local governments handle matters like waste management and local roads.

Second, Nigeria practices fiscal federalism, which involves the sharing of revenue between the federal, state, and local governments. The Revenue Mobilization Allocation and Fiscal Commission (RMAFC) determines how revenue from oil and other sources is shared among the three tiers of government.

However, Nigerian federalism faces several challenges. One major challenge is the issue of revenue allocation, as states with oil-producing resources often feel they should receive a larger share of oil revenue. Another challenge is the frequent conflicts between federal and state governments over issues like resource control and jurisdiction. The principle of derivation in revenue sharing has been a source of tension between oil-producing and non-oil-producing states.

Another challenge is the creation of new states. Since independence, Nigeria has created many new states from the original three regions, leading to increased administrative costs and potential ethnic tensions. The uneven development among states is also a challenge, as some states are more developed than others due to differences in resources and governance.

Ethno-religious diversity in Nigeria also presents challenges to federalism, as different groups may feel marginalized or underrepresented in the federal structure. The issue of local government autonomy has also been contentious, as state governments often control local governments, reducing their independence.

Class activity:
Students will debate whether the current federal structure in Nigeria adequately addresses the country's diversity and needs.

Evaluation questions:
1. Define federalism in the Nigerian context.
2. List three challenges of Nigerian federalism.
3. Explain how revenue allocation is a challenge in Nigerian federalism.
4. What is fiscal federalism and how does it operate in Nigeria?

Summary:
Federalism in Nigeria involves the sharing of power between the federal government and state governments, but it faces challenges like revenue allocation, uneven development, and managing the country's diversity.

topics.title: Constitution of Nigeria
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to identify the key features of the 1999 Constitution.
The students should be able to explain at least two amendments to the Nigerian Constitution.
The students should be able to differentiate between the different sections of the Nigerian Constitution.

Introduction:
We have studied Nigeria's federal system and leadership. Now we will examine the Nigerian Constitution, which is the supreme law of the land that governs how the country is run.

Content:
The current Nigerian Constitution is the 1999 Constitution, which was promulgated on May 29, 1999, when Nigeria returned to democratic rule after military dictatorship. The Constitution establishes Nigeria as a federal republic with a presidential system of government. It consists of a preamble, 7 parts, and 320 sections as originally enacted.

The Constitution is divided into several parts. Part I contains the provisions regarding the Federal Republic of Nigeria. Part II deals with the Fundamental Objectives and Directive Principles of State Policy. Part III outlines the Fundamental Rights of Nigerian citizens. Part IV establishes the Structure and Composition of the Legislative Houses. Part V deals with the Executive arm of government. Part VI covers the Judicial arm of government. Part VII contains Miscellaneous provisions.

The Nigerian Constitution has been amended several times since its promulgation. One significant amendment was in 2010, when the Constitution was amended to extend the tenure of local government chairmen and councilors from three to four years. Another important amendment was in 2011, which established the State Independent Electoral Commissions (SIECs) and the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) as independent bodies.

The 2015 amendment introduced the Not-Too-Young-To-Run bill, which reduced the age requirement for presidential candidates from 40 to 35 years, and for National Assembly members from 30 to 25 years. The 2018 amendment established the Federal Character Commission as a constitutional body to ensure fair representation of all ethnic groups in federal appointments.

The Nigerian Constitution also contains provisions for the creation of new states, the establishment of local governments, and the division of powers between the federal, state, and local governments. It outlines the powers and functions of the three arms of government - executive, legislature, and judiciary - and provides for checks and balances to prevent any arm from becoming too powerful.

The Constitution guarantees fundamental rights to Nigerian citizens, including the right to life, liberty, and fair hearing; freedom of thought, conscience, and religion; freedom of expression and the press; freedom of movement; and the right to own property. It also provides for the protection of minority rights and the promotion of social justice.

Class activity:
Students will work in groups to identify one fundamental right in the Nigerian Constitution and prepare a short presentation explaining its importance.

Evaluation questions:
1. When was the current Nigerian Constitution promulgated?
2. List two amendments to the Nigerian Constitution and explain their significance.
3. What are the Fundamental Rights guaranteed by the Nigerian Constitution?
4. Explain the structure of the Nigerian Constitution.

Summary:
The 1999 Constitution is the supreme law of Nigeria, establishing the country as a federal republic with a presidential system and guaranteeing fundamental rights to citizens, while also providing for amendments to adapt to changing needs.

topics.title: Midterm Test
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to demonstrate knowledge of topics covered in the first four weeks.
The students should be able to analyze and evaluate concepts discussed in class.

Introduction:
This week, we will assess your understanding of the topics we have covered so far through a midterm test. This will help me know how well you have grasped the content and identify areas that need more attention.

Content:
The midterm test will cover the following topics:
1. Nigeria in the 21st Century - Political, economic, and social developments
2. Leadership in Contemporary Nigeria - Past presidents and their impacts
3. Federalism in Nigeria - Meaning and challenges
4. Constitution of Nigeria - 1999 Constitution and amendments

The test will consist of multiple-choice questions, short answer questions, and one essay question. You will have 45 minutes to complete the test. Please read each question carefully before answering and manage your time wisely.

Class activity:
The midterm test will be administered during the regular class period.

Evaluation questions:
The midterm test will serve as the evaluation for this week.

Summary:
The midterm test will help assess your understanding of the topics covered in the first four weeks of the term.

topics.title: Elections and Electoral Bodies
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to identify the major electoral bodies in Nigeria.
The students should be able to explain the functions of INEC.
The students should be able to list at least three electoral reforms in Nigeria.

Introduction:
Following our midterm break, we will now examine elections and electoral bodies in Nigeria, focusing on the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) and electoral reforms that have shaped the country's democratic process.

Content:
Elections are a fundamental aspect of democracy, allowing citizens to choose their leaders and representatives. In Nigeria, elections are conducted by the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), which is established by the Constitution. INEC is responsible for the conduct of federal, state, and local government elections in Nigeria. It also registers political parties, voters, and candidates, and conducts voter education.

INEC has several key functions. First, it demarcates constituencies for elections to the National Assembly and state Houses of Assembly. Second, it conducts voter registration and maintains the voters' register. Third, it monitors elections to ensure they are free, fair, and transparent. Fourth, it resolves electoral disputes through its Electoral Tribunals. Fifth, it conducts voter education to inform citizens about their rights and responsibilities during elections.

Over the years, Nigeria has implemented several electoral reforms to improve the electoral process. One major reform was the introduction of the Smart Card Voter Registration System in 2011, which replaced the manual voter registration system. This system uses biometric technology to capture voters' fingerprints and photographs, reducing multiple registrations and impersonation.

Another important reform is the introduction of the Card Reader for accreditation during elections. The Card Reader verifies voters' fingerprints with the information stored in the Smart Card, preventing multiple voting and ensuring that only registered voters participate in elections.

The Electoral Act is another significant reform that has been amended several times to improve the electoral process. The 2022 Electoral Act introduced provisions for electronic transmission of election results, which aims to make the process more transparent and reduce manipulation of results.

Other electoral reforms include the establishment of the National Electoral Tribunal to resolve electoral disputes quickly, the introduction of gender quotas for political positions, and the regulation of campaign finance to reduce the influence of money in politics.

Despite these reforms, Nigeria's electoral process still faces challenges like vote buying, electoral violence, and manipulation of results. However, INEC and other stakeholders continue to work towards improving the electoral process to ensure that elections truly reflect the will of the people.

Class activity:
Students will role-play a mock election, taking on roles as INEC officials, candidates, voters, and observers to understand the electoral process.

Evaluation questions:
1. What are the functions of INEC in Nigeria?
2. Name three electoral reforms implemented in Nigeria.
3. How does the Smart Card Voter Registration System improve the electoral process?
4. Explain one challenge facing Nigeria's electoral process.

Summary:
The Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) is responsible for conducting elections in Nigeria, and various electoral reforms have been implemented to improve the electoral process and ensure free, fair, and credible elections.

topics.title: Midterm Break
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to rest and recharge for the second half of the term.
The students should be able to reflect on what they have learned so far.

Introduction:
This week is the midterm break, a time for rest and relaxation. After several weeks of intensive learning, it is important to take a break to recharge and return refreshed for the remaining part of the term.

Content:
The midterm break is an important period in the academic calendar. It provides an opportunity for students to rest, spend time with family, and engage in other activities outside of school. During this break, you should reflect on what you have learned so far in Nigerian History and identify areas where you need more understanding.

While the break is for rest, it is also a good time to revise the topics covered in the first six weeks of the term. You can review your notes, read additional materials, and prepare questions to ask when we resume classes. This will help you better understand the topics and be ready for new content when school resumes.

Class activity:
No formal class activity will be held during the midterm break. Students are encouraged to use this time for rest and revision.

Evaluation questions:
No formal evaluation will be conducted during the midterm break.

Summary:
The midterm break is a time for rest, reflection, and revision to prepare for the second half of the term.
